newsitem.title: UK: WW2 allies examining law on Nazi gold distribution.
newsitem.headline: WW2 allies examining law on Nazi gold distribution.

text.p: The United States, Britain and France have agreed not to distribute $68 million of gold looted by the Nazis until they establish whether it could be given to Holocaust survivors, British diplomatic sources said on Tuesday.

The gold is all that remains of 377 tonnes -- current value $4 billion -- recovered at the end of World War Two by allied forces. The rest has already been redistributed by a Tripartite Gold Commission (TGC).

The Simon Wiesenthal Centre, which hunts down alleged Nazi war criminals, has appealed to the TGC to share what remains among war victims, saying although some was looted from national banks, much came from people exterminated by the Nazis.
One British source said that under the agreement which set up the TGC, the gold should normally go to countries whose national banks were ransacked during the war.
But he added: "We are now looking to see whether there is any way we can overcome the legal and practical difficulties that distributing gold to individuals may involve."
He said Britain was also examining official archives to try to establish how much of the gold taken back by its forces at the end of the war was not "monetary gold", previously held by central banks.
"The indications at the moment are that there is not a vast amount," he said.
A report in Tuesday's New York Times said the Clinton administration believes there is new evidence to support claims that some of the gold belonged to Nazi death camp inmates.
"We (the U.S., Britain and France) have taken the first step, freezing the money in place," U.S. Under Secretary of Commerce Stuart Eizenstat told the paper.

The gold bars have been stored at the New York Federal Reserve Bank and the Bank of England, since Switzerland and Sweden turned them over to Allied powers, including France, at the end of the Second World War.
